Switch off ATP, considered proarrhythmic, and keep shocks only

False

New alert: "biventricular pacing 84%". She feels more breathless. Which measures can increase the proportion of biventricular pacing? (select all that apply)
options: Discuss restoring sinus rhythm (cardioversion, AF ablation)
Lengthen the device's sensed AV delay
Strengthen rate control (beta-blocker) if tolerated
Lower the lower rate to 50 bpm
commentaires: Correct: restoring sinus rhythm re-establishes atrial-synchronous pacing, with biventricular pacing at a short AV delay.
Incorrect: in AF there is no atrial tracking; the AV delay plays no role, and lengthening it in sinus rhythm would favour intrinsic conduction.
Correct: slowing AV conduction leaves more long cycles, on which biventricular pacing is delivered.
Incorrect: lowering the lower rate would leave even more room for intrinsic conduction.
cas-egmd-029.explication: The recording shows AF with fast, irregular conduction: most cycles are sensed (VS), and BV pacing occurs only after long cycles. In this patient with recent persistent AF and cardiomyopathy, a rhythm-control strategy (cardioversion after effective anticoagulation, AF ablation) should be discussed. AV delay or lower rate settings have no effect on conducted AF. Good habit: a fall in the biventricular pacing percentage should first prompt a search for AF or PVCs.

cas-egmd-029.rappel: The main causes of loss of biventricular pacing are conducted AF, frequent PVCs, an AV delay too long relative to intrinsic conduction, and sinus tachycardia above the upper tracking rate. Remote monitoring detects these falls early; they are associated with a higher risk of decompensation. In AF, options include intensified rate control, rhythm control (cardioversion, AF ablation, the latter recommended in selected heart failure patients by the 2024 ESC guidelines) and AV junction ablation.

cas-egmd-030.question: Follow-up visit for a 68-year-old man with a CRT-D who complains of increasing exertional breathlessness. The device technician shows you this real-time recording. Why is biventricular pacing delivered only on some cycles?

T-wave oversensing inhibiting pacing
Intrinsic conduction in AF, faster than pacing
Failure to mode switch, with atrial tracking of AF
commentaires: Incorrect: no pulse is delivered on the cycles marked VS, so this cannot be loss of capture.
Incorrect: no marker is placed on the T waves; the VS markers correspond to conducted QRS complexes.
Correct: in AF, most conducted QRS complexes occur before the pacing escape interval expires and inhibit CRT; only the long cycles leave room for BV pacing.
Incorrect: tracking AF would produce rapid BV pacing; here, pacing is infrequent and occurs after long cycles.
cas-egmd-030.explication: The atrial EGM shows rapid, disorganised activity (AF). Conducted QRS complexes occur irregularly, between ≈ 430 and 760 ms, and are sensed (VS): they inhibit pacing. Only the longer cycles allow the pacing interval to expire, hence a few isolated BV beats. There is therefore neither loss of capture (no pulse on VS cycles) nor atrial tracking of AF (the mode has switched). The problem is intrinsic AV conduction in AF, which deprives the patient of resynchronisation. Good habit: when a CRT device "is not pacing", look at the atrial rhythm first.
cas-egmd-030.aRetenir: CRT in AF: intrinsic conduction inhibits pacing, which occurs only after long cycles.
cas-egmd-030.rappel: A CRT device is a pacemaker: any ventricular activity sensed before the pacing interval expires inhibits it. In AF, the mode switches to non-tracking pacing (DDIR or VVIR) and biventricular pacing occurs only at the lower or sensor rate, or through regularisation algorithms. The clinical benefit of CRT falls clearly below 98% biventricular pacing. The percentage shown by the counter should be checked against the EGMs and, if needed, a Holter ECG.

cas-egmd-031.question: An 81-year-old man with a primary-prevention ICD and metastatic lung cancer is in a palliative care unit; he has clearly refused any resuscitation. He has just received this very painful shock in front of his distressed family. The on-call electrophysiologist can be reached. What is the most appropriate course of action?
options: Disable antitachycardia therapies, keeping pacing on
Leave the ICD active, as this shock was appropriate and effective
Schedule surgical explantation of the device as soon as possible
Also disable the device's bradycardia pacing
commentaires: Correct: in line with the patient's stated wishes, shocks are stopped (programmer, or a magnet in the meantime); painless pacing is kept for comfort.
Incorrect: the shock is appropriate, but it prolongs a dying process the patient does not want prolonged and causes him pain.
Incorrect: surgery is pointless; deactivation is done by programming, without any invasive procedure.
Incorrect: pacing causes neither pain nor prolongation of dying; stopping it could cause symptoms of bradycardia.
cas-egmd-031.explication: The episode shows VF (FS markers, disorganised EGMs), charging, an effective shock, then post-shock VVI pacing. The therapy is appropriate, but the context has changed: terminal illness, refusal of resuscitation, a shock experienced as suffering. Deactivating antitachycardia therapies is legitimate; it is neither assisted suicide nor euthanasia, but withdrawal of a treatment that has become disproportionate. In an emergency, a magnet placed over the device suspends shocks on most ICDs; permanent deactivation is done with the programmer. Pacing is usually maintained. Good habit: raise shock deactivation on admission to palliative care, not after the first shock.
cas-egmd-031.aRetenir: End of life: disable shocks (magnet in an emergency), keep pacing, in agreement with the patient.
cas-egmd-031.rappel: The 2010 HRS and EHRA consensus statements recognise the right of patients (or their representatives) to request deactivation of ICD therapies; this is withdrawal of treatment, which is ethically and legally acceptable. In France, the Claeys-Leonetti law governs the limitation and withdrawal of treatment. The discussion should ideally be anticipated, at implantation and again as the disease progresses. On most ICDs, a magnet suspends tachycardia detection without changing pacing, which allows action when no programmer is available.

cas-egmd-032.question: A 64-year-old woman has a dual-chamber ICD implanted for primary prevention (ischaemic heart disease, LVEF 30%). She arrives in the emergency department after three shocks in two hours, with ongoing chest pain; the ECG, in sinus rhythm, shows anterior ST-segment elevation. All the episodes look like this one. What is the priority?
options: Reprogram the VF zone to avoid further shocks
Catheter ablation of the VF substrate within the hour
Add ATP during charging in the VF zone
Urgent coronary angiography with a view to revascularisation
commentaires: Incorrect: the shocks are appropriate and protect her; it is the cause of the VF that must be treated.
Incorrect: ablation has no first-line role in VF related to acute ischaemia.
Incorrect: ATP does not terminate VF, nor does it treat the cause.
Correct: recurrent VF with chest pain and ST elevation requires urgent coronary angiography: acute ischaemia is the cause to treat.
cas-egmd-032.explication: The episode shows VF (disorganised EGMs, FS) correctly treated with a shock, followed by post-shock pacing. Three episodes of VF in two hours define an electrical storm; with ongoing chest pain and ST elevation, acute ischaemia is the most likely cause. The priority is urgent coronary angiography, together with beta-blockade, electrolyte correction and, if needed, amiodarone. The ICD therapies are appropriate and are not changed. Good habit: a storm of polymorphic VF calls for a search for acute ischaemia first.
cas-egmd-032.aRetenir: Recurrent VF with an acute coronary syndrome: urgent coronary angiography, without changing ICD therapies.
cas-egmd-032.rappel: Recurrent VF and polymorphic VT are often triggered by acute ischaemia, whereas monomorphic VT usually reflects scar-related re-entry. The 2022 ESC guidelines recommend urgent coronary angiography with revascularisation in patients with recurrent polymorphic VT or VF when acute ischaemia is suspected. The other storm measures (beta-blockade, sedation, correction of potassium and magnesium, amiodarone) are added. ICD interrogation confirms that the shocks were appropriate and identifies the arrhythmia.

cas-egmd-033.question: A 55-year-old man with ischaemic heart disease has a primary-prevention dual-chamber ICD and a private car licence. He received a shock during this episode last week. Since then: AF cardioversion under anticoagulation, beta-blocker increased, VT zone raised to 188 bpm with discriminators on; today's check is normal. He asks when he can drive again. What do you tell him?
options: Not for three months, as after any ICD therapy
Straight away, since the cause of the shock has been corrected
Never again: any shock permanently bans driving
Only after a normal defibrillation test
commentaires: Incorrect: the three-month restriction applies after appropriate therapy for a true ventricular arrhythmia.
Correct: after an inappropriate shock, driving can resume once the cause has been identified and corrected.
Incorrect: a permanent ban applies to group 2 licences, not to a private car licence after an inappropriate shock.
Incorrect: defibrillation testing adds nothing here: the problem was detection of AF, not shock efficacy.
cas-egmd-033.explication: The atrial EGM shows AF (rapid, disorganised activity); the Vs are irregular, between 300 and 440 ms, with the same morphology as the baseline rhythm on the shock EGM: this is fast AF conducted into the VT zone, and the shock was inappropriate. It does not reflect any risk of ventricular arrhythmia. The European consensus distinguishes the two situations: three months off driving (group 1) after appropriate therapy, but resumption as soon as the cause is corrected after inappropriate therapy. Here, the AF has been treated and the programming corrected: he may drive again. Good habit: first classify the therapy (appropriate or not), then apply the corresponding driving rule.
cas-egmd-033.aRetenir: After an inappropriate shock, driving (group 1) resumes as soon as the cause has been corrected.
cas-egmd-033.rappel: According to the 2009 EHRA consensus, endorsed by the 2022 ESC guidelines, group 1 drivers should refrain from driving for three months after appropriate therapy, but may resume driving after inappropriate therapy once the cause has been eliminated. Rapidly conducted AF is the leading cause of inappropriate shocks. Corrective measures include AF control (rate or rhythm), a higher detection zone (185–200 bpm in primary prevention), prolonged detection duration and discriminators active up to 200–230 bpm.

cas-egmd-034.question: A 56-year-old man with ischaemic heart disease (LVEF 30%) had a dual-chamber ICD implanted a month ago for primary prevention; VT zone from 150 bpm (400 ms) with discriminators, VF zone from 200 bpm. In cardiac rehabilitation, the team is worried about seeing this type of episode at every cycling session. What change do you suggest?
options: Switch off discriminators so as not to delay true therapy
Lower the VF zone to 170 bpm to separate the two zones better
Raise the detection zone to 185–200 bpm and prolong detection
Stop rehabilitation, which exposes him to inappropriate shocks
commentaires: Incorrect: the discriminators are what withheld therapy; switching them off would lead to treatment of this sinus tachycardia.
Incorrect: a VF zone at 170 bpm would shock exercise sinus tachycardia straight away, with no discrimination.
Correct: in primary prevention, the consensus recommends a lowest zone at 185–200 bpm with prolonged detection, which leaves exercise sinus tachycardia outside the zone.
Incorrect: rehabilitation is beneficial; it is the programming that must adapt to the patient.
cas-egmd-034.explication: The episode shows gradual 1:1 acceleration, each P preceding the QRS at a constant 150 ms interval with unchanged morphology: exercise sinus tachycardia entering the VT zone (TS) and then recognised by the discriminators (SVT marker). In a primary-prevention patient, a 150 bpm zone is unnecessarily low: it makes protection against inappropriate therapy depend entirely on the discriminators. The 2015 consensus, supported by MADIT-RIT and ADVANCE III, recommends a lowest zone between 185 and 200 bpm and a detection duration of at least 6–12 seconds (or 30 intervals), which reduces inappropriate therapy and even mortality. Good habit: in primary prevention, high zone and long detection.
cas-egmd-034.aRetenir: Primary prevention: lowest zone at 185–200 bpm and long detection, so that exercise sinus tachycardia is not treated.
cas-egmd-034.rappel: The 2015 HRS/EHRA consensus, confirmed by the 2019 focused update, recommends that in primary prevention the lowest tachycardia zone be programmed between 185 and 200 bpm (class I) with a prolonged detection duration (6–12 seconds or 30 intervals). MADIT-RIT showed that a high zone (≥ 200 bpm) or delayed detection reduced inappropriate therapy and mortality. ADVANCE III showed that detection at 30/40 intervals reduced therapies without more syncope. SVT–VT discriminators should remain active up to at least 200 bpm.

cas-egmd-035.question: A 48-year-old woman with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy has a dual-chamber ICD: VT zone from 150 bpm, discriminators applied only up to 180 bpm, VF zone from 220 bpm. This episode was recorded while cycling up a hill. True or false: if the sinus tachycardia had reached 190 bpm, the ICD could have delivered inappropriate therapy.
options: True
False
commentaires: Correct: above the discriminator upper limit (180 bpm), any tachycardia in the VT zone is treated; at 190 bpm, this sinus tachycardia would have received ATP, or even a shock.
Incorrect: discriminators are applied only up to the programmed limit; beyond it, sinus tachycardia is no longer protected.
cas-egmd-035.explication: On the tracing, the tachycardia accelerates gradually, 1:1, each P preceding the QRS by 150 ms with unchanged morphology: the discriminators recognise it as SVT (SVT marker) and withhold therapy. But they are applied only up to a programmable upper limit, here 180 bpm. In a young patient reaching high sinus rates on exertion, sinus tachycardia at 190 bpm would be above this limit and treated as VT. The consensus recommends applying discriminators up to 200 bpm, or even 230 bpm, and adapting the zones to age and activity. Good habit: check the discriminator upper limit in young and active patients.
cas-egmd-035.aRetenir: Above the discriminator upper limit, fast sinus tachycardia may be treated as VT.
cas-egmd-035.rappel: Each manufacturer applies SVT–VT discriminators up to a programmable limit (SVT limit, SVT upper limit, etc.), above which safety takes priority and any tachycardia is treated. The 2015 consensus recommends applying them up to 200 bpm (class I) and considers it reasonable to go up to 230 bpm. In young patients (hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, channelopathies), the maximum sinus rate must be taken into account: high zone, long detection, beta-blockade. An exercise test can help to check the programming.

cas-egmd-036.question: A 34-year-old man with Brugada syndrome has a dual-chamber ICD. He received a shock last night while asleep, with no preceding symptoms. In the emergency department he is in sinus rhythm and asymptomatic; interrogation shows this recording, which precedes detection. The electrophysiologist will not arrive for two hours. What is the immediate management?
options: Magnet over the device with monitoring and an external defibrillator ready
Intravenous isoprenaline to prevent a VF storm
Discharge home: appropriate shock for nocturnal VF
Urgent quinidine and transfer to intensive care
commentaires: Correct: the tracing shows T-wave oversensing, causing an inappropriate shock; the magnet suspends therapies until reprogramming, with monitoring.
Incorrect: isoprenaline treats VF storm in Brugada syndrome; here there is no VF but double counting.
Incorrect: the recording shows sinus rhythm at 78 bpm with every T wave counted; the shock was inappropriate and may recur.
Incorrect: quinidine prevents VF in Brugada syndrome; it does not correct oversensing.
cas-egmd-036.explication: The EGM shows sinus rhythm at 78 bpm (each P followed by a QRS, sinus shock EGM), but each cycle has two ventricular markers: VS on the QRS, then TS 300 ms later on a large T wave on the RV EGM, while the R wave is small. The ICD therefore counts a doubled rate and may meet detection criteria: this is T-wave oversensing, common in Brugada syndrome, where repolarisation is large and variable. The shock was inappropriate. While waiting for the electrophysiologist, therapies are suspended with a magnet, with monitoring and an external defibrillator ready, and the programming will then be corrected. Good habit: a "night-time" shock in Brugada syndrome is not necessarily VF: read the EGM.
cas-egmd-036.aRetenir: Two markers per cycle, one on the T wave: oversensing, inappropriate shock; magnet with monitoring until reprogramming.
cas-egmd-036.rappel: T-wave oversensing occurs when the T wave on the ventricular EGM exceeds the auto-adjusting sensitivity threshold, especially if the R wave is small (the starting threshold is calculated as a percentage of the R wave). It is favoured by channelopathies (Brugada, long or short QT), hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, hyperkalaemia and exercise. It is recognised by a marker at a fixed interval after each QRS, corresponding to the T wave, with a shock EGM showing sinus rhythm. Corrections include T-wave rejection algorithms, adjustment of the starting threshold or sensitivity decay delay, a change of sensing dipole and, if needed, lead revision.

cas-egmd-037.question: A 52-year-old woman with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy has a dual-chamber ICD; R wave measured at 2.5 mV. In clinic, the technician suggests correcting the phenomenon seen on this tracing by reducing RV sensitivity from 0.3 to 1.2 mV. True or false: this setting is risk-free, because VF EGMs are always much larger than the T wave.

False
commentaires: Incorrect: VF EGMs are often small and variable; with a 2.5 mV R wave, a sensitivity of 1.2 mV risks undersensing VF.
Correct: markedly reducing sensitivity risks undersensing VF; T-wave rejection algorithms or revision are preferred, and any reduction must be verified.
cas-egmd-037.explication: The RV EGM shows a small R wave and a large T wave, sensed 300 ms after each QRS (TS): T-wave oversensing. Reducing sensitivity makes the markers on the T wave disappear, but VF EGMs are fragmented, small and variable from cycle to cycle: with an R wave of only 2.5 mV, a sensitivity of 1.2 mV would leave an insufficient margin to detect VF. Safer solutions are T-wave rejection algorithms, adjusting the starting threshold or decay delay of auto-adjusting sensitivity, changing the sensing dipole (integrated bipolar) or repositioning the lead. If sensitivity is nevertheless reduced, VF detection must be checked. Good habit: oversensing is not corrected at the price of VF undersensing.
cas-egmd-037.aRetenir: Markedly reducing sensitivity risks VF undersensing: prefer dedicated algorithms or lead revision.
cas-egmd-037.rappel: ICDs use auto-adjusting sensitivity: after each sensed event, the threshold starts at a fraction of the R wave and then decays to the programmed maximum sensitivity (often 0.3 mV), so as not to miss VF signals. Reducing this maximum sensitivity lowers oversensing but also the ability to detect small VF EGMs. The 2015 consensus recommends using T-wave and oversensing rejection algorithms when available. A small R wave (below 3–5 mV) weakens all settings and should prompt discussion of lead revision.

cas-egmd-038.question: A 68-year-old man has a dual-chamber ICD implanted 11 years ago. He received four shocks in ten minutes while putting his shopping away on a high shelf. In the emergency department he is alert and in sinus rhythm; here is the onset of one of the episodes. Which immediate measures are appropriate? (select all that apply)
options: Re-enable the ICD at discharge, as noise is often transient
Suspend therapies (magnet or programming) with monitoring
Check the RV lead pacing and shock impedances
Give amiodarone to prevent further episodes
commentaires: Incorrect: a lead producing noise, especially with arm movements, needs revision; re-enabling it as it is would lead to further shocks.
Correct: the shocks are being delivered for lead noise; they must be suspended immediately, with monitoring and an external defibrillator ready.
Correct: an abrupt impedance change (often a rise) confirms conductor damage and guides revision.
Incorrect: there is no ventricular arrhythmia to prevent; amiodarone has no effect on lead noise.
cas-egmd-038.explication: The atrial EGM and the shock EGM show regular sinus rhythm at 72 bpm, while the RV EGM shows bursts of very rapid, non-physiological signals counted as FS. Good habit: noise on the RV EGM alone with a normal shock EGM = lead problem until proven otherwise.
cas-egmd-038.aRetenir: Shocks due to lead noise: suspend therapies with monitoring, check impedances, revise the lead.
cas-egmd-038.rappel: Lead noise appears as very rapid, irregular, non-physiological signals, often intermittent and sometimes triggered by arm movements or breathing. It is confined to the channel using the damaged conductor, while the shock EGM (far field) remains normal. Associated signs are an abrupt change in pacing impedance, very short V-V intervals (< 130–150 ms) and repeated non-sustained episodes. The 2015 consensus recommends activating lead integrity alerts and noise rejection algorithms. Correction requires implantation of a new lead.

cas-egmd-039.question: A 63-year-old woman has a Medtronic dual-chamber ICD. CareLink alert: "Lead Integrity Alert"; she says she heard her device "beep" the day before. She has had no shock. Here is one of the transmitted episodes. Which change did the device apply automatically when this alert was triggered?

It switched RV sensing to unipolar tip-to-can
It reduced ventricular sensitivity to its minimum value
It extended the number of intervals required to detect VF
commentaires: Incorrect: the device never disables therapies by itself; the patient remains protected.
Incorrect: an ICD cannot sense in unipolar tip-to-can configuration; this is not the algorithm's response.
Incorrect: the algorithm does not change sensitivity, which would risk VF undersensing.

cas-egmd-039.explication: The RV EGM shows bursts of non-physiological signals counted as FS, while the shock EGM and the atrial EGM remain sinus: RV lead noise. cas-egmd-039.aRetenir: Lead Integrity Alert (Medtronic): VF detection extended to 30/40 and an audible alert; lead revision still has to be arranged.
cas-egmd-039.rappel: The Lead Integrity Alert, developed after the Sprint Fidelis lead fractures, combines several criteria: abnormal or abruptly changed pacing impedance, a high number of very short V-V intervals (sensing integrity counter) and very fast non-sustained episodes. When at least two criteria are met, the device extends VF detection to 30/40 intervals and issues an audible and remotely transmitted alert. The 2015 consensus recommends activating these lead alerts (class I).

cas-egmd-040.question: A 61-year-old man with ischaemic heart disease has had a dual-chamber ICD for 9 years; he is not pacing-dependent. cas-egmd-040.explication: The bursts of non-physiological signals appear only on the RV EGM, while the atrial EGM and the shock EGM show regular sinus rhythm: the noise comes from the RV lead. cas-egmd-040.aRetenir: Noise on the RV EGM with soaring impedance: lead fracture, requiring replacement.

Combined with noise on the near-field EGM, it confirms lead dysfunction. Management is surgical: addition of a new defibrillation lead, with or without extraction of the old one. Until then, noise rejection algorithms, extended detection and close remote monitoring limit the risk of inappropriate shock.
